issues.issue: The party is identified with misspellings ("Thornas Skold", "Bjormo Gard"), so the identity/address of the individual contracting party is stated inaccurately on the face of the instrument. A court could be asked whether the named individual is the person bound.

The recital identifies the Original Agreement, which Section 9.12 both supersedes and partly preserves through its proviso for prior agreements filed with the USPTO. Whether the recited Original Agreement survives in any respect cannot be settled from the recital alone.

Clause (iii) of the control test contains an unmatched closing parenthesis and dangles into "of the equity having the power to vote", so it is unclear whether the lesser-percentage rule qualifies (i) and (ii) or stands alone. The punctuation changes what ownership threshold makes a Person an Affiliate.

"Books and Records" is defined by reference to records "related to the Restoraderm Technology or the Purchased Assets," while Section 2.1(b) makes the Books and Records themselves part of the Purchased Assets. The definition is circular as to its own boundary.

"Additional Records" ends in an open catch-all ("such as, but not limited to") after enumerating batch protocols, sterility protocols, clinical trial documentation and marketing materials, with no principle limiting the general words. What must be handed over under Section 8.5 therefore has no fixed boundary.

"Commercially Reasonable Efforts" closes with "and other relevant factors," leaving the standard without any measurable benchmark. Because it governs the diligence obligations in Sections 3.4, 3.7 and 3.6, its content is the natural subject of dispute.

The definition excepts terms of the Agreement "disclosed pursuant to Section 7.5 herein," but Section 7.5 is the Limitation of Liabilities clause and authorizes no disclosure; the disclosure provision is Section 6.5. The cross-reference cannot be given effect as written.

"Control" is defined "with respect to Technology and/or Patent Rights," but "Technology" is capitalized as a defined term and is nowhere defined in Article 1. The reach of Control (and hence of Restoraderm Know-How under 1.21) is left uncertain.

"First Commercial Sale" requires a sale after Regulatory Approval "if applicable," without saying who decides when approval is applicable. For a topical product marketed without FDA approval it is unclear whether a First Commercial Sale can occur at all, which drives the US$700,000 payment in Section 2.3(c).

After a list of specific catastrophes the definition adds "or other similar event, beyond the reasonable control of such Party," a catch-all whose scope against the enumerated specifics is undefined. It also conditions the whole definition on undefined "reasonable efforts to avoid such occurrence."

"Know-how" lists "inventions" and "data" twice and ends with the unbounded word "information," so it embraces anything at all with no confidentiality or subject-matter limit. Its outer edge matters because 1.21 assigns all Skold Know-How relating to the Restoraderm Technology.

"Losses" excludes "special, consequential, indirect, punitive, provisional or similar damages"; "provisional" damages is not a recognized category and "similar damages" has no boundary. What a Party may recover as Losses is therefore uncertain.

After seven enumerated deductions, item (h) permits "any other similar and customary deductions taken in accordance with GAAP," a catch-all sitting against the specifics. Whether a given deduction is "similar and customary" is exactly what a royalty dispute would turn on.

"Patent Rights" covers "all patents and patent applications and all patent applications hereafter filed" with no owner, subject-matter or time limit stated in the definition itself. Whether later-filed applications of either Party fall within it is unresolved.

"Product" means "a product incorporating the Restoraderm Technology," with no measure of how much of that technology must be incorporated or whether a reformulated or later-improved delivery system still counts. Royalties under 4.2, milestones under 4.1 and the Term under 8.1 all turn on this word.

"Restoraderm Intellectual Property" is confined to Patent Rights, Know-How and related causes of action and omits Trademarks, even though Section 1.26 defines "Trademark" for use somewhere in the instrument. Read with Section 2.1, this leaves ownership of the Restoraderm name unallocated.

"Restoraderm Know-How" is frozen at Know-How owned or Controlled "as of the Effective Date," while Section 2.5 purports to assign to CollaGenex all know-how Skold later develops relating to the Restoraderm Technology. Which instrument governs post-closing know-how cannot be resolved from this definition alone.

"Restoraderm Patent Rights" is limited to rights owned or Controlled by Skold as of the Effective Date and keyed to Schedule 1.22, yet Section 2.3(c) contemplates a patent issuing later and Section 4.2 pays royalties only on Products covered by a Valid Claim of these rights. Whether later-filed or later-issued patents fall inside the defined set is left open.

"Restoraderm Technology" is defined as the topical drug delivery technology "developed by Skold and covered by the patent applications recited in Schedule 1.22," so it is unclear whether the technology is limited to what those three applications claim or extends to the wider delivery platform. "Topical" is bounded only negatively, by excluding oral, nasal and intravenous use.

"Sublicense Income" is limited to "royalties actually received ... on account of sales of Products," which by expressio unius excludes upfront fees, milestones and other sublicense consideration. What a sublicensee pays outside a per-sale royalty escapes Section 4.3 entirely.

"Trademark" is defined but the defined term appears nowhere in the operative provisions, so the definition has no work to do unless trademarks are read into the Purchased Assets. Whether the Restoraderm mark was conveyed under Sections 1.20 and 2.1 is left to be argued from this orphan definition.

"Valid Claim" is defined by reference to a claim that "but for the licenses granted herein, would be infringed," yet Article 2 effects an outright assignment and this Agreement grants CollaGenex no license. The premise of the definition cannot be squared with the transaction structure in Section 2.1.

The Purchased Assets are exhaustively enumerated in (a)-(d) and do not include Trademarks or the Restoraderm name, though Section 1.26 defines "Trademark" and Section 2.2 lists only books and records as Excluded Assets. Whether the name passed with the "goodwill, if any, relating to the foregoing" is the very question the two provisions leave open.

The Excluded Assets are said to be "specifically enumerated" yet consist only of books and records Skold must keep by law or for accounting, so anything of Skold's not caught by Section 2.1's list is allocated by neither provision. The boundary between what is retained and what is sold is left to inference.

Subsection (c) is self-contradictory: payment falls due thirty days after patent issuance "provided such issuance occurs after the First Commercial Sale," then thirty days after the First Commercial Sale if the patent issues first, and never if no patent issues. Read with the sole-discretion deemed-launch sentence, when (and whether) the US$700,000 becomes payable is genuinely uncertain.

Section 2.4 obliges Skold to use "all reasonable efforts," a standard different from the defined "Commercially Reasonable Efforts" used throughout Article 3, with nothing to say whether the two differ. The measure of Skold's post-closing cooperation duty is left unfixed.

The present assignment sweeps in all intellectual property Skold develops "relating to the Restoraderm Technology or any other topical drug delivery technology" during the term of this Agreement or the Consulting Agreement, an open-ended field far wider than the Purchased Assets defined in Section 2.1. Neither "any other topical drug delivery technology" nor the end date of the capture period is bounded.

The membership sentence is garbled: each Party appoints two persons, but "in addition to Skold, Skold shall appoint an advisor or other designee," leaving unclear whether Skold's side is two members or three. Because voting is one vote per representative with a CollaGenex tie-break, the composition affects every decision.

The Committee is to "review and agree upon the Products to be developed" and the Development Plans, which cannot be squared with Section 3.2(b) and Section 3.3 giving CollaGenex the final decision on both. Whether the Committee's agreement is a condition or a formality is unresolved.

A meeting requires "at least two (2) committee members of each Party" and treats unanimous action as duly taken, which sits badly with Section 3.1(a) giving CollaGenex a tie-breaking vote on all decisions. Whether the Committee can act other than unanimously is left contradictory between the two subsections.

The provision runs on "working days," a unit found nowhere else, while Section 1.4 defines "Business Day" and directs that any reference to "day" means a calendar day. Which measure governs the twenty- and ten-day notice periods is unstated.

The final sentence directs that "the Joint Development Committee shall meet in order to review such proposal," but no such body exists; Section 3.1 creates only the Joint Steering Committee. The proposal review step is assigned to a non-existent committee.

This subsection gives CollaGenex "the final decision as to whether and which Products are developed," which cannot be squared with Section 3.1(c)(i) requiring the Joint Steering Committee to review and agree upon the Products to be developed. The two provisions allocate the same decision to different bodies.

The sentence conflates a right and a duty — "sole responsibility and use its Commercially Reasonable Efforts for developing Products" — so it is unclear whether CollaGenex must develop any Product or merely controls development if it chooses to develop. The diligence obligations in Section 3.4 are the only concrete measure.

Development Plans go to the Joint Steering Committee "for review and approval" while the same sentence gives CollaGenex "final-decision making authority with respect to any element of a Development Plan." The approval requirement and the final-authority proviso cannot both be given full effect.

"Initiate development efforts on at least five Products" fixes no content for what counts as initiating development, and the obligation is further softened by the "Commercially Reasonable Efforts" preamble. Whether the December 31, 2005 obligation was met is unmeasurable on these words.

The abandonment proviso lets CollaGenex drop a Product before spending US$75,000 and says the abandoned Product "shall not count as one of the five Products," without saying whether a replacement Product must then be started or the March 31, 2007 deadline re-run. The diligence obligation and the escape hatch are not reconciled within the subsection.

The Clobetasol credit deems paragraphs (a) and (b) satisfied for one Product and reduces the requirement to "four (4) more Products," but leaves the December 31, 2005 and March 31, 2007 dates in place and says nothing about the BPO Product identified in Section 3.2(b). Whether the reduced obligation carries the original deadlines is unstated.

Skold must render "such assistance, as may be reasonably requested or required by CollaGenex" with no limit on quantity, duration or compensation, and no stated relationship to the separate Consulting Agreement under Section 2.5. The extent of the unpaid assistance duty is open.

CollaGenex acts "at its sole discretion and expense" yet "shall use Commercially Reasonable Efforts" to prosecute and maintain the patent rights — a discretion and a mandatory standard in the same sentence. Because the US$700,000 under Section 2.3(c) depends on a patent issuing, whether CollaGenex owed an enforceable prosecution duty is contestable.

CollaGenex must use Commercially Reasonable Efforts "to market and sell all Products" and prepare a Business Plan, but no timing, content or minimum standard for the Plan is given and CollaGenex alone decides which Products exist. The marketing obligation has no measurable content.

The opening sentence promises Milestone Payments "with respect to each of the first five Products," while the closing sentences limit them to "the first five Products with different active ingredients." The same provision states two different populations of paying Products.

Milestone (a) is triggered by CollaGenex's "receipt of data, in a form acceptable to CollaGenex," making the payment condition entirely subjective to the payor. Whether that acceptance is constrained by good faith is left unsaid.

Royalties are due only on Products "covered by a Valid Claim of the Restoraderm Patent Rights," but Section 1.22 freezes those rights at the Effective Date and Schedule 1.22 lists only pending applications, while Section 1.27 requires an issued unexpired claim. Read together, the royalty may never accrue at all.

The third-party stacking offset stops where royalties would fall "below half the royalty earned," and "the royalty earned" is not tied to any stated figure. Whether the floor is half of 5% of Net Sales or half of some other measure is ambiguous.

This section promises 25% of "all Sublicense Income," but Section 1.24 counts only royalties received on a sublicensee's sales, so lump-sum and milestone sublicense consideration falls outside the payment obligation. The generality here and the narrowness of the definition cannot both be given effect.

The 30% set-off runs against "amounts that are otherwise due Skold under this Article 4" with no cap or time limit, and its interaction with the royalty floor in Section 4.2 (not below half the royalty earned) is unaddressed. Whether the two reductions stack is unresolved.

The report's contents are numbered with two items labelled "(iv)", so the enumeration is defective on its face. It is unclear whether the Sublicense Income item and the exchange-rate item are separate requirements.

All payments are reduced by amounts "required to be paid or withheld pursuant to any applicable law," borne solely by Skold, with no gross-up and no mechanism for treaty relief for a Swedish resident. Whose tax and which law may trigger the reduction is left at large.

The exchange-rate source is described as the "Dollar spot forward against the Dollar" table in The Financial Times, a self-referential and incorrect table name. The conversion mechanism therefore identifies no ascertainable rate source unless the Parties agree another publication.

Records need only be kept "for a period of two (2) years after the date of the invoice," while audits may reach books for any year ending up to twenty-four months before the request and may be exercised only once a year. The retention window and the audit window do not line up, so records may lawfully be gone before an audit right is exercised.
